newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Nov 13.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Nov 13.

text.p: - Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- MAJOR THREATENS SHOWDOWN OVER EU SOCIAL POLICY

John Major, criticising a European Court rejection of a UK challenge to an EU working week directive, has warned that unless concessions are received on the issue Britain will veto any intergovernmental conference review of the Maastricht treaty. The European Court decided that Britain must proceed with the implementation of a 48-hour working week, a decision which John Major stated had gone against the spirit of what Britain had signed up to at Maastricht when it obtained an opt-out from the social chapter.
-- SOCIETIES WARN OF DELAY TO FLOTATIONS

Four building societies preparing to convert to bank status have warned that their plans may be delayed as a result of uncertainty over proposed legislation for the sector and disputes over how they should treat disabled account holders in their entitlement to free shares. Building societies legislation was last month dropped from the government's schedule. Delays in this area have made it impossible for the societies concerned to issue detailed information regarding their conversions.
-- BRITAIN TO SHAKE UP ITS OVERSEAS TELECOMS MARKET

It is believed that Britain will issue licenses to all 46 companies that have applied to compete with British Telecom and Mercury Communications in the provision of full international telecoms services in the UK. Till now rivals of the two have had to rent lines from the companies. The licensing decision will allow competitors to establish their own infrastructures. It is believed the decision could go some way towards easing concerns expressed by AT&T about the recent deal between BT and MCI.
-- FRENCH INSURANCE MERGER TO CREATE 12 BILLION STG GROUP

Two of the largest insurance companies in France, Axa and UAP, have announced that they are to merge. The deal will create the second-largest insurance group in the world with a turnover of some 36 billion stg and will go some way to addressing the perception of French financial services being weak. The merger also comes as part of a process of consolidation among major players in the sector globally.
-- TRIBUNAL OVERTURNS BAN ON BARINGS MANAGER

Ron Baker, the former head of derivatives trading at the collapsed Barings Bank, has won a challenge to a proposal from the Securities and Futures Authority that he be banned from working in a senior position in the industry for three years. A number of other managers implicated in the collapse of the bank have already received lengthy bans. The tribunal did, however, reprimand him over his failure to correctly monitor one aspect of the trading at the Singapore branch of the bank that went disastrously wrong.
-- DR SOLOMON IN RACE TO FLOAT ON EASDAQ

The British anti-virus software company, Dr Solomon, is making preparations to be the first company to float on a European version of the US Nasdaq high-technology stock exchange - the Easdaq. The company hopes to raise 52 million stg in such a flotation, scheduled for late November. French and Belgian companies are also vying to be the first to embark on such an issue, however. It is anticipated that up to 50 companies could launch of the Easdaq within 12 months.
-- EU IMPROVES TELECOMS TALKS OFFER

The European Union on Tuesday lodged what was described as a "substantially improved" offer to the US in talks on the liberalisation of their respective telecommunications markets. Talks have been taking place in Geneva between trade representatives from both the US and EU in an effort to re-start stalled World Trade Organisation negotiations on a wider agreement. The decision by Spain to open its markets to competition by 1998 formed the major part of the improved EU offer. The US is expected to respond in kind.
-- RISK OF MAIL STRIKE AT CHRISTMAS LIFTED

Union representatives and management from the Royal Mail have reached a compromise agreement in their long-running dispute over the introduction of new working practices in Britain's postal services. As part of the deal reached workers will receive an immediate 3 percent rise in pay, while the issue of working practices is assessed by joint management/union working parties. The dispute had threatened to affect Christmas deliveries and raised the prospect of the government lifting for an extended period the Royal Mail's monopoly on the delivery of letters.
-- BRITISH GAS PULLS OUT OF OFFSHORE TAX BATTLE

British Gas has withdrawn a demand for the repayment of one billion sterling paid in offshore taxes. The company had previously claimed to have found a loophole in the gas levy imposed by the government on North Sea gas field production, but following talks with the Department of Trade and Industry announced that in fact the law had been correctly drafted and applied. The dispute had threatened to cause chaos in the entire gas production sector.
-- PFI LENDERS 'GET NO EXTRA PROTECTION'

The government has announced that it will not be introducing additional guarantees for banks considering making loans to hospital trusts taking part in private finance initiative projects. The chief executive of the Private Finance Panel, David Steeds, noted that the risks involved in such transactions were already adequately covered by existing legislation. Banks have been wary of entering into lending to hospital trusts for construction projects because of concerns about security for such long-term initiatives.
